followUps:
A Node is any object in the DOM tree; an Element is a Node that came from a tag. Text, comments and the document itself are Nodes but not Elements.

For <p>Hi <b>you</b></p>, the p has 2 child nodes (a text node and the b element) but 1 child element. Element adds tag APIs such as classList, querySelector and children; every Element is a Node, not the reverse.

The CSSOM is the browser's tree of parsed CSS rules, built next to the DOM from stylesheets and inline styles. It is what document.styleSheets and el.style expose.

The browser combines the DOM and CSSOM into a render tree that holds only visible elements with their computed styles (display: none nodes are left out). Then it does layout (sizes, positions) and paint. Scripts can change either tree, which triggers new style, layout or paint work; CSS also blocks rendering until it is parsed.

Because childNodes includes every kind of node, while children contains only elements.

Take <ul> <li>A</li> <li>B</li> </ul>. The whitespace between tags becomes text nodes, so childNodes.length is 5 (3 text nodes plus 2 li) but children.length is 2. Comments also count in childNodes. Also, childNodes is a live NodeList and children a live HTMLCollection.

code.title: Live vs static collections

followUps:
Walk the tree from a root and collect every element whose class list contains the name; a recursive or stack walk visits each node once, so it is O(n).

function byClass(root, c, out = []) {
  if (root.classList && root.classList.contains(c)) out.push(root);
  for (const k of root.children) byClass(k, c, out);
  return out;
}

This returns a static array. A real HTMLCollection is live, so browsers cache the result and invalidate it when the tree changes.

closest(selector) starts at the element itself and walks up through its ancestors, returning the first one that matches the selector, or null.

Its main use is event delegation: if a click lands on an icon inside <button class="del">, event.target.closest('button.del') gives the button. It checks the element first, then the parent, then the grandparent, so it costs O(depth). Always handle null, and check the result is inside your container.

Because a shadow root is a separate, encapsulated tree, and document.querySelectorAll only searches the light (normal) tree.

Elements inside <my-card>'s shadow root are hidden from outside selectors, which is the point of encapsulation (styles and ids cannot clash). To reach them, call host.shadowRoot.querySelectorAll(...) on an open root; closed roots return null for shadowRoot. Selectors do not pierce boundaries, and slotted children stay in the light tree.

code.title: Capture, target and bubble phases

followUps:
In current browsers, capture listeners on the target run first, then the normal (bubble) ones, regardless of the order in which you added them.

If you add a normal listener and then a capture listener on the same button, the capture one still runs first (Chrome 89+ and the updated DOM spec). Older browsers ran them in registration order at the target. The demo above shows the target phase is a single stop where both kinds fire.

Events such as focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave, load, scroll (on elements) and unload do not bubble. The alternatives are bubbling siblings or capture.

  • focusin / focusout instead of focus / blur
  • mouseover / mouseout instead of mouseenter / leave
  • or listen in the capture phase: addEventListener('focus', fn, true)

Check event.bubbles to see which kind you have.

Call event.composedPath() inside a listener; it returns an array of the nodes the event will travel through, from the target up to window.

For a click on a button in a div in body you get [button, div, body, html, document, window]. It also includes nodes inside open shadow roots and respects retargeting, which event.target does not. Call it during dispatch; after dispatch it returns an empty array.

code.title: preventDefault vs stopPropagation

followUps:
It fails when the event is not cancelable or when the listener is passive; the call is then ignored (Chrome logs a console warning for passive ones).

event.cancelable is false for some events, such as most scroll events. A listener added with { passive: true } promises not to cancel, and touchstart / wheel listeners on window, document and body are passive by default. Fix: use { passive: false } or CSS touch-action. Calling it after the default already ran (for example inside a timeout) is also too late.

In jQuery, return false in a handler calls both preventDefault() and stopPropagation(). With addEventListener, a returned false does nothing at all.

Only the old inline form onclick="return false" (and el.onclick = ...) cancels the default, and it does not stop propagation. So when copying jQuery code to plain JavaScript, write the two calls explicitly, and prefer only preventDefault().

Check event.defaultPrevented; it is true once any listener has called preventDefault() on a cancelable event.

link.addEventListener('click', e => {
  if (e.defaultPrevented) return; // someone handled it
  e.preventDefault();
  route(link.href);
});

This is how routers and analytics code avoid double handling. It only helps for listeners that ran earlier, so order matters; dispatchEvent also returns false when the event was cancelled.

code.title: Event delegation with closest()

followUps:
Use the bubbling mouseover / mouseout events on the container, because mouseenter and mouseleave do not bubble.

list.addEventListener('mouseover', e => {
  const row = e.target.closest('tr');
  if (row && list.contains(row)) row.classList.add('hot');
});

Pair it with a mouseout listener that removes the class. Check e.relatedTarget to ignore moves between children of the same row, otherwise the highlight flickers. For pure styling, CSS :hover needs no JavaScript.

React attaches one native listener per event type to the root container and decides which of your handlers to call, which is delegation.

When you click a button, the native event bubbles to the root. React finds the component path from the target fiber, runs onClickCapture handlers top down, then onClick handlers bottom up, passing a SyntheticEvent. That is why it does not attach one listener per JSX element, and why handlers added or removed in re-renders need no manual cleanup.

Skip delegation when the event does not bubble, when you need stopPropagation per element, or when there are only one or two targets.

  • Non-bubbling events (load, scroll, mouseenter) where capture is awkward
  • Very hot events like mousemove over a huge container: the handler runs for every move and filtering costs time
  • One button: a direct listener is simpler and clearer

form.submit() sends the form immediately without validation and without firing the submit event; form.requestSubmit() behaves like a real click on the submit button.

With requestSubmit(), the browser runs built-in validation (required, pattern), fires submit so your listener can call preventDefault(), and only then submits. You can pass a submit button to include its name and value. Use requestSubmit() in code, and avoid submit() unless you want to skip all handlers.

Unchecked checkboxes are left out of FormData entirely, and repeated names appear once per value.

For <input type=checkbox name="tag" value="a" checked> and an unchecked value="b", fd.getAll('tag') returns ['a'] and fd.has('tag') is true; if none are checked, fd.get('tag') is null. Object.fromEntries(fd) keeps only the last value of a repeated name, so use getAll for multi-value fields. Disabled inputs are also skipped.

Tie each message to its field, announce it to screen readers, and move focus to the first error.

  1. Use a real <label for> for each input.
  2. Set aria-invalid="true" and aria-describedby="id-of-error" on the bad input.
  3. Put the message in text next to the field (not colour alone); a summary region with role="alert" is read aloud.
  4. Call firstInvalid.focus() after submit.

Clear the attributes when the value becomes valid.

No, not really: insertAdjacentHTML parses a string as HTML exactly like innerHTML, so it has the same XSS risk. It is only a bit faster because it does not rebuild the existing children.

Inserting <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> runs the handler either way. Safe options for untrusted text are insertAdjacentText, textContent or createElement. Use the HTML versions only with trusted or sanitised strings.

Yes, a hardcoded template with no outside data is safe, because an attacker cannot change the string.

el.innerHTML = '<b>Saved</b>' is fine. The danger starts the moment you interpolate something dynamic, such as `<b>${name}</b>`, since name might contain markup. Data that came from a database or URL counts as outside data even if it looks harmless. It still replaces all children, which drops listeners and state on them.

React escapes every value you put in JSX, so text is rendered as text, never parsed as HTML.

<p>{comment}</p> shows <img onerror=...> literally. The escape hatch is dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }}, which inserts raw HTML and is as risky as innerHTML, so sanitise first (DOMPurify). Other holes: href={userUrl} with a javascript: URL, and rendering server HTML unsanitised.

code.title: Debounce vs throttle with a fake clock

followUps:
Nothing is debounced: each render makes a new debounced function with its own timer, so every call starts a fresh independent timer and all of them fire.

Typing 5 letters runs the handler 5 times, once per timer, just delayed. Fix it by keeping one instance across renders: useMemo(() => debounce(fn, 300), []), useRef, or a useDebouncedValue hook, and cancel it in the effect cleanup on unmount. Watch out that the stored function may capture stale props.

maxWait guarantees the function runs at least once every maxWait ms even if calls never pause, by also remembering when the first pending call happened.

if (!first) first = now;
clearTimeout(timer);
const left = Math.min(wait, maxWait - (now - first));
timer = setTimeout(run, left); // run() resets first

With wait 300 and maxWait 1000, a user typing nonstop still gets a call at about 1000 ms. This is lodash's behaviour, and it is how debounce becomes throttle-like.

Because requestAnimationFrame runs once per screen refresh, right before painting, so work is never done more often than the user can see.

On a 60 Hz screen that is about every 16.7 ms. A scroll handler firing 200 times a second would do 200 updates; with rAF you store the latest value and update once per frame (about 60). It also pauses in background tabs. Use time-based throttle for non-visual work like network calls.

code.title: A small EventEmitter

followUps:
Split the pattern on : and compare segment by segment, treating * as matching any one segment. On emit, call listeners of the exact name and of every matching pattern.

function match(pat, name) {
  const p = pat.split(':'), n = name.split(':');
  return p.length === n.length &&
    p.every((s, i) => s === '*' || s === n[i]);
}

match('cart:*','cart:add') is true and match('cart:*','user:add') is false. Cost is O(number of patterns) per emit, or use a trie for many.

In observer, the subject knows its observers and calls them directly; in pub/sub, a broker (channel) sits between publishers and subscribers, so they do not know each other.

A button with addEventListener is observer. A message bus where one module publishes "order:paid" and others subscribe by topic is pub/sub. Pub/sub decouples more, can work across processes (queues) and filters by topic, but is harder to trace and debug.

Always unsubscribe when the owner goes away; the emitter holds a reference to every listener, so the listener and everything it captures cannot be garbage collected.

  • Keep the unsubscribe function returned by on and call it on unmount or close.
  • Use once for one-shot events.
  • Use an AbortController signal to remove many listeners at once.
  • Watch the listener count (Node warns above 10 per event).

code.title: Microtask timing: user click vs click()

followUps:
Later: setTimeout callbacks are tasks (macrotasks), so they run after the whole current task and all microtasks, even with a delay of 0.

With a timeout added in the first listener, a real click prints: first, micro, second, then timeout. With button.click(): first, second, script ends, micro, then timeout. The order is: current task, then all microtasks, then the next task. A timeout never runs between listeners of one event.

Nothing changes in the order of calls, but the microtask checkpoint still happens between any two listeners for a real click, wherever they are.

Say the first listener is on the button and the second on its parent div. For a real click the stack is empty after the button's listener, so the microtask runs before the div's listener. For click() from script, all listeners on the path run first and the microtask runs at the end. The path (capture, target, bubble) decides the listener order, not the microtasks.

await pauses only that listener; the rest of its code becomes a microtask, and the browser immediately goes on to the next listener, which does not wait for it.

btn.onclick = async () => { log('a1'); await 0; log('a2'); };
btn.addEventListener('click', () => log('b'));

For a real click the output is a1, a2, b (the checkpoint runs between listeners). For click() from script it is a1, b, a2. The event does not wait for async listeners, and preventDefault() after an await comes too late.

With the old design (listeners on document), two React versions on one page, or React next to other code, interfered with each other's events, and stopPropagation could not work across them.

Attaching to each app's root container means multiple React roots (and micro-frontends) get their own isolated delegation, and non-React code between roots behaves normally. It also made gradual upgrades possible and let a native e.stopPropagation() inside a React tree stop events from reaching document listeners.

A portal renders children into a different DOM node, but events still bubble through the React tree, so a parent component hears events from a portal child even though the DOM nodes are far apart.

A modal rendered into document.body via createPortal still makes its click bubble to the component that rendered it, so an onClick on that parent fires. Native listeners follow the DOM tree and will not see it that way. Stop it in the modal with e.stopPropagation() if the parent should not react.

Add a document listener inside useEffect and ignore clicks that happen inside the element, using a ref and contains.

useEffect(() => {
  const h = e => { if (!ref.current?.contains(e.target)) onOut(); };
  document.addEventListener('pointerdown', h);
  return () => document.removeEventListener('pointerdown', h);
}, [onOut]);

Use composedPath() for shadow DOM and portals, add the listener only while open, and handle Escape too.

code.title: Layout thrashing: interleaved vs batched

followUps:
Reading geometry such as offsetWidth, offsetHeight, offsetTop, clientHeight, scrollTop, getBoundingClientRect() and getComputedStyle(el).height forces the browser to calculate layout first if styles changed.

If you just changed el.style.width and then read el.offsetHeight, the browser must do the layout right away instead of waiting for the frame. Doing this per item in a loop of 100 elements costs 100 layouts instead of 1, as shown in the demo.

Open the Performance panel, record while you reproduce the problem, and look for long tasks, purple Layout blocks and dropped frames; for field data use INP.

  1. Recording shows tasks over 50 ms as red-flagged long tasks.
  2. Repeated Layout entries with a "forced reflow" warning point to thrashing.
  3. INP (Interaction to Next Paint) from the web-vitals library or CrUX; under 200 ms is good.

The Lighthouse and Performance Insights panels give a quick summary.

Because the browser tells you when an element enters the viewport, so your code does not run on every scroll event and does not force layout.

const io = new IntersectionObserver(es => es.forEach(e => {
  if (e.isIntersecting) { e.target.src = e.target.dataset.src; io.unobserve(e.target); }
}));
imgs.forEach(i => io.observe(i));

A scroll handler fires dozens of times a second and calls getBoundingClientRect on every image; the observer works asynchronously off the main path. (Plain loading="lazy" needs no JavaScript.)

Use the Event Listeners panel, or temporarily wrap stopPropagation to print a stack trace when it is called.

const orig = Event.prototype.stopPropagation;
Event.prototype.stopPropagation = function () {
  console.trace('stopPropagation', this.type, this.currentTarget);
  return orig.apply(this, arguments);
};

The trace shows which file and line called it, and currentTarget shows the element. Do the same for stopImmediatePropagation. You can also search the bundle, and set a capture listener on window to compare what it sees.

getEventListeners(el) is a Chrome DevTools console helper that returns an object listing the listeners on el, grouped by event type.

getEventListeners(button).click gives an array of entries with listener, useCapture, passive and once. You can call .listener to run it or removeEventListener to remove it for an experiment. It exists only in the DevTools console (not in page code), and it only sees listeners on that element, not on ancestors.

Click the real element as a user would and assert on the visible result, instead of calling the handler yourself.

// Testing Library
await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }));
expect(onSave).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
// Playwright
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();

Playwright checks that the element is visible, enabled and not covered by an overlay before clicking, so an invisible overlay failure shows up as a timeout with a clear log. That catches exactly this bug class.

Transient user activation is a short-lived flag that the browser sets when the user really interacts with the page (click, key press, touch); it lets sensitive APIs run for a moment afterwards.

It lasts a few seconds (about 5 s in Chrome; the spec leaves it to the browser) and is consumed by some APIs such as window.open popups. You can check navigator.userActivation.isActive. A button handler can open one popup; a timer started 10 seconds later cannot.

No: isTrusted is an unforgeable property set by the browser itself, and scripts cannot assign it (it is a read-only property on the event, set to false for events made by script).

Writing new MouseEvent('click', {isTrusted: true}) is ignored and the result is still false. Only the user agent, reacting to real hardware or OS input, creates events with true. Extensions and automation tools (DevTools protocol, WebDriver) can inject real input at the browser level, which is why those tools are not a script in the page.

You cannot open a real file dialog from a test script, so set the file directly on the input instead of clicking the button.

// Playwright
await page.setInputFiles('input[type=file]', 'fixtures/a.png');
// or catch the chooser
const [chooser] = await Promise.all([
  page.waitForEvent('filechooser'),
  page.click('#upload')]);
await chooser.setFiles('fixtures/a.png');

Testing Library's userEvent.upload(input, file) does the same in jsdom. Then assert on the preview or request.

composed: true lets an event cross the shadow boundary and keep bubbling into the outer document; retargeting means that outside the shadow root, event.target is rewritten to the host element.

A click on a button inside <my-menu>'s shadow root, seen by a listener on document, has target equal to my-menu, hiding internals. Inside the shadow tree the real button is the target. Custom events default to composed: false and bubbles: false, so set both when you want outsiders to hear them.

Use event.composedPath() instead of event.target, because the target is retargeted to the shadow host and a plain contains check can wrongly say the click was outside.

document.addEventListener('pointerdown', e => {
  if (!e.composedPath().includes(popup)) close();
}, { signal: ac.signal });

The path includes nodes inside open shadow roots. Add the listener only while the popup is open and abort it on close. Closed shadow roots hide their inner nodes from the path.

No: a global event bus hides who talks to whom and shares one namespace across teams, so it is risky for a shared library.

Names can clash ("close" from two libraries), nothing is typed, and memory leaks are easy because subscribers must unsubscribe. Prefer events dispatched on the component's own element (custom events with a documented name and payload), callbacks or props, and a scoped emitter that the app passes in. A bus is fine inside one app you control.
